experiments.name: ALU-path chain
experiments.command: ./bench --method slope --unroll 800 --unroll2 1600 --iters 40 --warmup 10 --reps 7 --init 'addi.d $r20, $sp, -1088; li.d $r22, -64; and $r20, $r20, $r22; li.d $r4, 8; st.b $r4, $r20, 0; li.d $r4, 0; st.b $r4, $r20, 8; li.d $r13, 0' --asm 'ld.bu $r4, $r20, 0; add.d $r20, $r20, $r4'

latencies.notes: The chain ld.bu + add.d measures 5.94 cycles. One cycle is the add.d and one more is what the ALU consumer path pays over the address path, so 2 are subtracted and the load latency is 4, the same as the bare ld.d pointer chase (3.94-3.98). A 8-bit load cannot be chased directly because its result is not a complete address, and the width does not change the latency: every width reads the same chain. The ALU path itself is 5. The buffer holds 8 and 0 so the chase stays inside one cache line.

throughput.name: 8 independent lanes
throughput.command: ./bench --unroll 1000 --iters 1000 --warmup 10 --reps 5 --core 0 --init 'addi.d $r20, $sp, -1024' --asm 'ld.bu $r12, $r20, 0; ld.bu $r13, $r20, 8; ld.bu $r14, $r20, 16; ld.bu $r15, $r20, 24; ld.bu $r16, $r20, 32; ld.bu $r17, $r20, 40; ld.bu $r18, $r20, 48; ld.bu $r19, $r20, 56'
